title: Cabinet Raises EPFO Wage Ceiling to ₹25,000 After 12 Years
excerpt: The Union Cabinet's decision to lift the mandatory EPFO coverage ceiling from ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 a month will bring over 51 lakh more workers into provident fund, pension and insurance coverage from September 17.
body:
• The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Wednesday approved raising the wage ceiling for mandatory EPFO coverage from ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 a month — the first revision in 12 years.
  • The move is expected to bring more than 51 lakh additional employees in the ₹15,000–₹25,000 wage band under statutory provident fund, pension and insurance coverage.
  • The revised ceiling takes effect on 17 September, coinciding with Vishwakarma Diwas and Seva Diwas. Annual government outgo is estimated at ₹11,339 crore, or about ₹56,696 crore over five years.
  • Employers face higher PF, pension and EDLI contributions, and employees in the affected bracket will see slightly lower take-home pay — the trade-off for stronger retirement savings.

The Union Cabinet has approved raising the wage ceiling for mandatory coverage under the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation from ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 a month, a decision expected to bring more than 51 lakh additional employees into India's statutory social security net. The move, announced by Union minister Ashwini Vaishnaw on Wednesday after a Cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, is the first revision of the ceiling in 12 years.

The ceiling had remained unchanged from 2004 to 2014, when it was raised to ₹15,000 in September 2014 — and stayed there since, even as wages, minimum wages and living costs rose substantially.

Context & Background

At present, a fresh employee joining work at wages above ₹15,000 a month is not automatically covered under the EPF framework and can remain outside mandatory provident fund, pension and associated insurance protection. Raising the ceiling pulls workers in the ₹15,000–₹25,000 band into the statutory net.

Union minister for labour and employment Mansukh Mandaviya put the rationale plainly: the ceiling no longer matched reality. "Today, the average income of a regular salaried employee is around ₹23,000, while minimum wages, including for unskilled workers, have crossed ₹15,000 in several states," he said. "As a result, a fresh employee joining employment at a wage above ₹15,000 is not automatically covered under EPF and is also not eligible for pension benefits under EPS." The proposal went through inter-ministerial consultations and was recommended by the Expenditure Finance Committee on 16 June before Wednesday's Cabinet approval.

Impact & Analysis

The decision expands access to three pillars of EPFO coverage: provident fund savings, pension protection under the Employees' Pension Scheme (EPS) and insurance protection under the Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme (EDLI). EPFO currently serves about 79.8 crore contributing members across 768,000 establishments, per its dashboard, while EPS provides pensions to around 8.2 million pensioners.

"The decision will provide employees with the benefits of provident fund savings, pension and insurance protection. It is a major step towards providing social security to all workers under the Labour Codes and will also give further impetus to the formalisation of employment."

— Mansukh Mandaviya, Union Minister for Labour and Employment

"The move will help create a more level playing field, as compliant staffing firms already provide EPF, EPS and EDLI benefits, while the higher threshold could narrow the cost arbitrage available to unorganised players," said Suchita Dutta, executive director of the Indian Staffing Federation.

There is a cost. The annual government outgo is estimated at about ₹11,339 crore against existing budgetary support of roughly ₹10,250 crore, with five-year expenditure of approximately ₹56,696 crore. Employers will carry higher PF, pension and EDLI contributions, "particularly for employees currently drawing wages between ₹15,000 and ₹25,000 where contributions are restricted to the statutory ceiling," said Puneet Gupta, partner, People Advisory Services-Tax, EY India.

"Employees in the affected salary bracket are also likely to witness a reduction in take-home pay due to the higher employee PF contribution."

— Puneet Gupta, partner, People Advisory Services–Tax, EY India

Diaspora Angle

The impact on Indians abroad is indirect but real: many NRIs hold dormant EPF accounts from earlier stints in India, and families back home in the ₹15,000–₹25,000 band — often first-generation formal workers — now gain retirement savings, pension eligibility and insurance protection they previously fell just outside of. Anyone advising relatives on Indian employment contracts should factor the new ceiling into offer evaluations.

What's Next

The revised ceiling comes into effect on 17 September — aligned by the government with Vishwakarma Diwas, associated with artisans and skilled workers, and Seva Diwas, observed on the Prime Minister's birthday. The Ministry of Labour and Employment and EPFO will now take the statutory and administrative steps to implement the decision.

Employers with payrolls in the ₹15,000–₹25,000 band should prepare for higher statutory contributions and communicate the take-home impact; newly covered employees will gain EPF interest accruals, EPS pension rights and EDLI-linked insurance from the effective date, subject to scheme provisions. The data to watch: EPFO's membership additions in the months after implementation — the real test of whether the 51-lakh estimate materialises.
